extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate discrete mathematics and computer science students and instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for representing discrete-mathematical objects (sums, counting problems, and graphs) and for storing graphs/data structures in linear computer memory; includes problem-solving heuristics and specific memory-layout formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mathematical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Levi used mathematical induction-style arguments in his proofs and was one of the first to use induction (300 years before Pascal); he used induction specifically to prove formula (C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use induction when a statement naturally decomposes into a clear base case and an inductive step; induction can yield short, clear proofs (as for (C)). Consider whether induction is the most natural method — some identities (like (A) and (B)) may be easier by pairing or algebraic rearrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing tricks for summations
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove sums by pairing terms from front and back (e.g., pairing 1 with n, 2 with n-1) to reduce a sum to a small number of identical pair-sums. Levi uses pairing to prove triangle-number identities and other lemmas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pairing turns long sums into multiples of a common value; useful for consecutive integer sums and certain symmetric sums. Look for natural pairings (front/back or left-group/right-group) as a first approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rearrangement arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove identities by rearranging terms (e.g., grouping and reordering elements to reveal simpler sums); Levi uses rearrangement for some lemmas and square-pyramid identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rearrangement is effective when ordering reveals cancellation or repeated patterns; explicitly show how rows/columns or blocks rearrange to expose known sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic expansion (FOIL and multiplication out)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use algebraic expansion (e.g., FOILing, multiplying out polynomials) to prove inductive lemmas and to transform summation expressions into closed forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When algebraic manipulation is straightforward and mechanical, expansion can quickly verify equalities or inductive steps. Use it to turn summation formulas into polynomial closed forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial interpretation of sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret numeric sequences combinatorially (e.g., triangle numbers count pairs chosen from n; square counts in grids correspond to sums of squares; rectangles correspond to sums of cubes via combinatorial reasoning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate algebraic formulas into counting arguments — combinatorial meaning often suggests direct bijections or simple counting proofs and can reveal why an identity holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gather data and experiment to conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Before tackling counting problems, compute small cases and tabulate values (by hand or via a program) to look for patterns. Writing a program can generate more data and reveal structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use computed examples to form conjectures, test patterns, and guide the choice of proof technique. Programs are useful but not necessary; they can suggest organized ways to think about the counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize counting by size or type (case decomposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count combinatorial objects by size, orientation, or other natural types (e.g., triangles in a triangular grid counted by size and whether they point up or down).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partition the set of objects into disjoint, easily countable classes to avoid omissions and to reveal patterns summing to known sequences (like triangular numbers by rows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive and unravel recurrence relations
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct closed forms are not obvious, derive recurrence equations (possibly with parity-separated recurrences) and 'unravel' them into summations that can be simplified to closed form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recurrence relations as an intermediate step: establish base cases, derive the recurrence, then iterate/unfold the recurrence to get summations and simplify using known identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast proof styles pedagogically
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple proofs (induction, pairing, rearrangement, algebraic manipulation) for the same identity to compare techniques and discuss why a particular method was chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the classroom, present Levi's multiple proofs as exercises; encourage students to analyze pros and cons of symbolic algebra vs Euclid-style prose and to debate methodological choices (Pólya-style guided discovery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Locator functions for vectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Map vector elements to memory addresses via a locator function: addr(i) = α + (i-1)s where α is the address of the first element and s is the storage size per element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this formula to compute addresses for linear arrays; the system decides α and the programmer uses the offset formula. Ensure correct indexing convention (0- or 1-based) consistent with language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locator functions for matrices (row-major mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Map matrix element a_{i,j} to memory with a locator function that stores rows contiguously: addr(i,j) = α + (i-1)r*s + (j-1)s where r = n*s (number of storage locations per row), α is address of A_{1,1}, and s is storage size per element. (Row-major order is commonly used.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and document whether row-major or column-major ordering is used; use the appropriate formula to compute offsets. This gives contiguous sequential storage of a row followed by the next row.

rubrics_metrics.name: Row-major vs column-major order choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Row-major order stores successive row elements contiguously; column-major stores column elements contiguously. The text notes row-major is commonly used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about order because it affects address calculations and performance (cache locality). Match the order to language conventions and algorithms that traverse rows or columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linked lists / pointer abstraction (Treasure Hunt analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Store each datum together with a pointer to the next datum (linked list). The Treasure Hunt game illustrates storing data plus a pointer; the system chooses physical addresses, programmers reason with abstract links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent linked structures by links/pointers rather than concrete addresses in diagrams. Programmers should treat pointers abstractly and not rely on fixed addresses; linked lists are good when insertion/deletion flexibility is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjacency matrix representation for graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: For an n-vertex graph, define adjacency matrix A with entries a_{ij} = 1 if i adjacent to j, else 0; matrix operations (multiplication, transposition) can be used to analyze graphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use adjacency matrices for dense graphs and when matrix algebra is useful. Be aware of O(n^2) space cost and implications for large/sparse graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vector-based adjacency list representation (e and p vectors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Store all adjacency entries in a single vector e listing adj(1), adj(2), ... and a pointer/index vector p where p[i] gives the start index in e of adj(i); p has length n+1 (extra sentinel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This representation uses |e| = 2|E| entries and |p| = n+1. It is memory-efficient for sparse graphs and useful in languages without pointers (COBOL, FORTRAN). Degree(i) = p[i+1]-p[i].

rubrics_metrics.name: Linked adjacency lists (per-vertex linked lists)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each vertex v, store adj(v) as a linked list; maintain a vector of n pointers to the heads of these lists. This representation makes adding and deleting edges easy and is commonly used in graph algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use linked adjacency lists for sparse graphs and dynamic graphs where edge insertions/deletions are frequent. Requires pointer support; diagrams show links rather than absolute addresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space/time tradeoffs between representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare adjacency matrix (size ~n^2), vector-based adjacency list (size ~2|E| + (n+1)), and linked adjacency lists (pointer overhead) and choose representation according to graph density and language constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use adjacency matrix for dense graphs or when matrix computations are needed; use adjacency lists for sparse graphs. Consider language features (presence/absence of pointers) and operations required (fast adjacency test vs fast iteration over neighbors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Locator functions as the central mapping concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Locator functions map elements of a discrete structure to specific memory addresses and are the foundation of formula-based representations of vectors and matrices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing memory layouts, explicitly define locator functions and the constants (α, s, row-size) they use; document indexing conventions and storage unit sizes to avoid off-by-one and alignment errors.
